questions.stem: What is the very first step in every patient assessment?
questions.why: BSI comes before anything else — assume any and all bodily fluid is potentially harmful before making patient contact.

options.t: Checking the Glasgow Coma Scale
options.why: GCS is part of the disability assessment, several steps after the very first action.

options.t: Determining the field impression
options.why: A field impression comes only after gathering assessment data, not before scene safety.

options.t: Obtaining a SAMPLE history
options.why: History taking happens later in the assessment sequence.

options.t: Body substance isolation

questions.stem: What does the 'N' in the scene size-up mnemonic ENAMES stand for?
questions.why: N stands for number of patients — establishing early whether this is a single patient or a multi-casualty incident.

options.t: Nature of illness
options.why: Nature of illness is a separate consideration, distinct from the letter N in this mnemonic.

options.t: Neurologic status
options.why: Neurologic status is assessed later, in the primary survey, not the scene size-up.

options.t: Necessary equipment only
options.why: This mnemonic covers scene factors broadly, not an equipment-only checklist.

options.t: Number of patients

questions.stem: What does the 'E' at the end of ENAMES (extrication) affect?
questions.why: A long or difficult extrication bumps up the acuity of the call — prolonged entrapment carries its own physiologic risk.

options.t: A long extrication increases the call's overall acuity
It sets how long you have before requesting additional units
options.why: Resource requests come from the whole scene picture; this letter is about what a prolonged entrapment does to the patient.

options.t: It solely determines which hospital receives the patient
options.why: Hospital destination is driven by other trauma criteria, not extrication time alone.

options.t: It tells you which extrication tools the responding engine carries
options.why: Equipment is a rescue consideration. In the size-up, extrication time is weighed for its effect on patient acuity.

questions.stem: Scene safety assessment should be treated as what kind of process?
questions.why: Scene safety is continuous — providers must stay aware of their environment and always have an exit plan throughout the call, not just at the start.

options.t: Optional if the dispatch information sounded benign
options.why: Dispatch information can be incomplete or wrong, so safety assessment can't be skipped.

options.t: A single check performed only on arrival
options.why: A one-time check on arrival misses changes in the environment as the call unfolds.

options.t: Something delegated entirely to law enforcement
options.why: Providers remain responsible for their own ongoing scene safety, not just law enforcement.

options.t: Continuous, throughout the entire call

questions.stem: What is assessed first in the primary survey to judge how well the brain is functioning?
questions.why: Responsiveness/LOC — via AVPU and A&O status — is assessed first to gauge how well the brain itself is functioning.

options.t: Responsiveness and level of consciousness
Bilateral breath sounds heard on the chest
options.why: Lung sounds are assessed in the breathing component, a separate primary survey step.

options.t: The patient's complete medication list
options.why: A medication list is gathered during history taking, later in the process.

options.t: The current blood glucose level
options.why: BGL is checked but isn't the primary survey's first responsiveness assessment.

questions.stem: Once a life threat is identified during the primary survey, when should it be managed?
questions.why: Life threats are managed immediately, as they're found — airway, decompression, and bleeding control don't wait for the rest of the assessment to finish.

options.t: After obtaining verbal consent from a family member
options.why: Immediate life threats are managed without waiting on that kind of consent process.

options.t: Only once IV access has been established
options.why: IV access is not a prerequisite for managing an identified life threat like an airway or bleeding problem.

options.t: Only after the full secondary assessment is finished
options.why: Waiting for the secondary assessment to finish delays management of something already identified as life-threatening.

options.t: Immediately, as soon as it's found

questions.stem: What determines how the airway should be opened in a trauma patient?
questions.why: Suspected spinal injury changes which airway maneuver is safe to use, favoring a jaw thrust over techniques that extend the neck.

options.t: Whether a spinal injury is suspected
The patient's stated pain level
options.why: Pain level doesn't determine which airway-opening technique is used.

options.t: The patient's approximate age alone
options.why: Age alone doesn't dictate the maneuver — suspected spinal injury does.

options.t: Whether the patient has a documented allergy list
options.why: An allergy list is unrelated to the choice of airway maneuver.

questions.stem: In the breathing assessment, what should prompt immediate initiation of oxygen therapy?
questions.why: Oxygen therapy is started immediately when the breathing assessment shows it's needed, and injuries compromising breathing are managed right away.

options.t: Only after a complete SAMPLE history has first been gathered
options.why: A SAMPLE history is not a prerequisite for starting oxygen when it's clearly needed.

options.t: Waiting until the secondary assessment has been fully completed
options.why: Delaying oxygen until the secondary assessment risks worsening hypoxia unnecessarily.

options.t: Findings on the breathing assessment that show it is needed
Only once a full 12-lead ECG has actually been performed
options.why: A 12-lead is unrelated to and shouldn't delay oxygen therapy decisions.

questions.stem: What skin-sign pattern is associated with a cardiac cause of poor perfusion?
questions.why: Diaphoretic (sweaty) skin is the pattern associated with a cardiac cause of poor perfusion, distinct from the grey of acidosis or the mottled look of systemic shock.

options.t: Diaphoretic skin
Mottled skin
options.why: Mottling reflects sluggish flow through the peripheral capillary beds — the systemic pattern rather than the cardiac one.

options.t: Flushed, dry skin
options.why: Flushed, dry skin points toward heat exposure or an anticholinergic picture, not a perfusion failure.

options.t: Grey skin
options.why: Grey skin tracks with acidosis, where poor perfusion has already shifted the patient's metabolism.

questions.stem: Grey, diaphoretic, and mottled skin each point somewhere different. What makes that set useful during assessment?
questions.why: Different skin-sign patterns point toward different underlying causes of poor perfusion — acidosis, cardiac, or systemic — helping narrow the field impression.

options.t: They confirm the diagnosis without needing vital signs
options.why: Skin signs narrow the field impression — they never replace vitals or the rest of the assessment.

options.t: They help localize the likely underlying cause of poor perfusion
They grade how severe the shock is on a three-point scale
options.why: The patterns point toward a cause rather than measuring severity: grey suggests acidosis, diaphoretic a cardiac cause, mottled a systemic one.

options.t: They only appear once the patient has stopped compensating
options.why: Skin changes are among the earliest perfusion findings — they show up well before decompensation.

questions.stem: What is assessed under 'disability' in the primary survey?
questions.why: Disability in the primary survey means a neuro evaluation — pupils, GCS, and checking for gross neurologic deficits like movement, strength, and sensation in all extremities.

options.t: Neuro status, including gross deficits and movement in all limbs
The patient's job and any functional disability status they have
options.why: Employment or social disability status is not part of this clinical assessment step.

options.t: The structural condition of the ambulance's own equipment
options.why: Equipment integrity has nothing to do with the disability step of patient assessment.

options.t: Whether the patient already has a preexisting physical disability
options.why: A preexisting disability history is gathered separately, not as this primary survey component.

questions.stem: What type of questions are generally preferred when taking a patient history?
questions.why: Open-ended, non-leading questions let the patient describe their own experience without the provider inadvertently shaping the answer.

options.t: Questions read entirely off of a rigid, fixed script
options.why: A rigid fixed script works against the natural, patient-specific flow that open-ended questioning allows.

options.t: Questions phrased to suggest the answer you already expect
options.why: Leading questions risk skewing the patient's own account of what happened.

options.t: Open-ended questions that avoid leading the patient's answer
Only yes and no questions, purely to keep things efficient
options.why: Yes/no questions can be a useful shortcut in some situations but aren't the generally preferred default approach.

questions.stem: When taking a history from an unresponsive patient, what should you do?
questions.why: If the patient can't give information, other sources — family, friends, bystanders, medical alert devices — become the way to gather that same history.

options.t: Rely only on whatever the patient's ID badge happens to say
options.why: An ID badge alone is a poor substitute for the richer information available from bystanders and family.

options.t: Skip history taking entirely, since the patient can't respond
options.why: History taking doesn't stop just because the patient can't speak for themselves.

options.t: Use other sources — family, bystanders, or medical devices
Wait until the patient wakes up before gathering any history
options.why: Waiting for consciousness could mean losing critical time-sensitive information.

questions.stem: What should an unresponsive patient's assessment specifically include that a responsive patient's might not need in the same way?
questions.why: Since an unresponsive patient can't self-report, a physical head-to-toe exam becomes essential to find what a verbal history would otherwise reveal.

options.t: A discussion of the chief complaint in the patient's own words
options.why: An unresponsive patient can't describe a chief complaint in their own words.

options.t: A head-to-toe exam
A conversation about medication compliance
options.why: Medication compliance is usually discussed verbally with a responsive patient, which isn't possible here.

options.t: An assessment of orientation to person, place, and time
options.why: Orientation checks require a responsive patient who can answer questions.

questions.stem: Why should nonessential people be removed during sensitive history-taking when possible?
questions.why: Removing nonessential people protects patient privacy around sensitive topics and can make the patient more willing to disclose accurate information.

options.t: To protect privacy and reduce the odds of withheld information
Because it's a strict legal requirement in absolutely every case
options.why: This is a judgment-based best practice, not framed as an absolute universal legal mandate.

options.t: Because doing so speeds up documentation once the call is done
options.why: Documentation speed isn't the stated reason for this practice.

options.t: Because any bystander present is automatically a safety threat
options.why: Bystanders being present isn't itself framed as a universal safety threat — privacy is the concern here.

questions.stem: What is a differential diagnosis in the context of prehospital assessment?
questions.why: A differential diagnosis is a working hypothesis — the provider's best current thinking about what's causing the patient's presentation, subject to revision as more information comes in.

options.t: A working hypothesis of what the patient's problem might be
A list of the medications the patient currently takes daily
options.why: A medication list is part of SAMPLE history, a different piece of information entirely.

options.t: A billing code that gets assigned sometime after transport ends
options.why: A billing code is an administrative artifact, not a clinical hypothesis.

options.t: A confirmed, final diagnosis that gets made right in the field
options.why: Field impressions are working hypotheses, not confirmed final diagnoses — that requires further hospital workup.

questions.stem: Which history-taking mnemonics might be used together to build a complete picture of a patient's complaint?
questions.why: Depending on the presentation, SAMPLE, OPQRST, and DCAP-BTLS (among others like AEIOU-TIPS) can each contribute a different layer to a complete assessment.

options.t: Only a single mnemonic should ever be used on any given call
options.why: Multiple mnemonics can be layered depending on what the specific presentation calls for.

options.t: None at all — mnemonics are actively discouraged in practice
options.why: These mnemonics are actively used tools in real assessment, not discouraged.

options.t: Only SAMPLE, since that alone is thought to cover everything
options.why: SAMPLE alone doesn't capture everything — OPQRST expands the pain history and DCAP-BTLS structures the physical exam.

options.t: SAMPLE, OPQRST, and DCAP-BTLS, depending on the presentation

questions.stem: What does the secondary assessment generally include?
questions.why: The secondary assessment layers on vital signs and a full systemic physical exam, going beyond the primary survey's rapid life-threat check.

options.t: Solely the patient's insurance information
options.why: Insurance information has no place in this clinical assessment step.

options.t: Only a repeat of the primary survey
options.why: The secondary assessment builds on, rather than simply repeating, the primary survey.

options.t: Only a review of past medical records
options.why: Past medical records aren't the defining content of the secondary assessment — the physical exam and vitals are.

options.t: Vital signs and a systemic physical exam

questions.stem: What is meant by 'pertinent negative' in documentation?
questions.why: A pertinent negative is a relevant finding you specifically checked for and did not find — like the absence of chest pain in a cardiac workup — and it's still worth documenting.

options.t: A relevant finding that is notably absent on exam
A lab result reported as within normal limits
options.why: A normal lab value is a different kind of documentation than a pertinent negative exam finding.

options.t: A finding that turned out to be clinically insignificant
options.why: A pertinent negative is specifically significant — the opposite of insignificant.

options.t: Any negative comment a patient makes about their care
options.why: This is a clinical documentation term, unrelated to a patient's comments about their care.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of orthostatic vital signs?
questions.why: Orthostatic vitals — BP and pulse taken in different positions — help reveal volume depletion and how well the systemic circulation is compensating.

options.t: To measure blood pressure only while the patient lies flat
options.why: Orthostatics specifically involve a position change, not a flat-only measurement.

options.t: To take the place of a standard set of primary vital signs
options.why: Orthostatic vitals supplement, rather than replace, standard vital signs.

options.t: To specifically diagnose a particular cardiac dysrhythmia
options.why: Orthostatics assess volume status and compensation, not dysrhythmias directly.

options.t: To assess volume depletion and how well the system compensates

questions.stem: Auscultation with a stethoscope during the secondary assessment is primarily used to evaluate what?
questions.why: Auscultation with a stethoscope during the secondary assessment is used to evaluate lung sounds.

options.t: Skin turgor
options.why: Skin turgor is assessed by palpation and inspection, not auscultation.

options.t: Range of motion in joints
options.why: Range of motion is assessed through movement and palpation, not listening.

options.t: Pupil response
options.why: Pupil response is a visual assessment, not something auscultated with a stethoscope.

options.t: Lung sounds

questions.stem: What does a rapid full-body scan in the secondary assessment generally cover?
questions.why: The rapid full-body scan is meant to be broad — skin, nails, head, eyes/ears, nose, and throat are explicitly part of that quick systemic sweep.

options.t: Only the chest and abdomen
options.why: Limiting the scan to the chest and abdomen misses other regions the full-body scan is meant to cover.

options.t: Only areas the patient specifically points to as painful
options.why: Relying only on where the patient points can miss silent but significant findings elsewhere.

options.t: Skin, nails, head, eyes/ears, nose, and throat
Only the extremities, skipping the trunk and head
options.why: Skipping the trunk and head would leave major regions of the rapid scan unexamined.

questions.stem: What does a field impression represent?
questions.why: The field impression is the provider's own working determination of what they believe the patient's problem is, based on the assessment so far.

options.t: The provider's own determination of what they think is going on
A diagnosis finalized once the patient reaches the hospital
options.why: A finalized diagnosis is a hospital-level determination, not what a field impression represents.

options.t: A legal document that requires the patient's own signature
options.why: A field impression isn't a legal document requiring patient signature.

options.t: A billing classification assigned sometime after the call
options.why: Billing classification is an administrative step unrelated to the clinical field impression.

questions.stem: What does 'big sick versus little sick' help determine?
questions.why: 'Big sick versus little sick' is a quick severity gestalt that drives the transport decision — how urgently and how the patient needs to move.

options.t: The patient's insurance eligibility for the ambulance ride
options.why: Insurance eligibility has no connection to this clinical severity assessment.

options.t: The transport decision and the overall urgency of the call
The exact hospital bed the patient will end up assigned to
options.why: Hospital bed assignment is a receiving-facility administrative decision, not this field judgment.

options.t: Which specific medication should ultimately be administered
options.why: Medication choice depends on the specific presentation, not this general sick/not-sick framework alone.

questions.stem: For a priority patient, what is the general approach to on-scene interventions?
questions.why: Priority patients get only what's truly necessary on scene, with the rest of the assessment and care continuing during transport.

options.t: Complete the secondary assessment on scene, then move
options.why: The secondary can be done en route; holding a priority patient on scene for it delays definitive care.

options.t: Complete every possible intervention before ever moving the patient
options.why: Completing everything on scene before moving delays transport for a patient who needs rapid definitive care.

options.t: Wait for a second unit before beginning transport
options.why: Waiting on another unit adds scene time — a priority patient goes as soon as the necessary interventions are done.

options.t: Do only what is necessary on scene; the rest happens en route

questions.stem: What does reassessment involve after initial patient contact?
questions.why: Reassessment means repeating the primary survey, repeating vital signs, reviewing what interventions have been done, and notifying the hospital of updates.

options.t: Repeating the primary survey, vitals, and reviewing interventions
Only rechecking vitals, while skipping the primary survey part
options.why: Reassessment includes repeating the primary survey itself, not just vital signs alone.

options.t: Something that only applies once a patient visibly worsens
options.why: Reassessment happens routinely, not only when the patient visibly worsens.

options.t: A one-time check performed only at the very end of the call
options.why: Reassessment is an ongoing process, not a single check saved for the end of the call.

questions.stem: Why is repeating the primary survey part of ongoing reassessment, even after it was already done once?
questions.why: A patient's status can deteriorate or change over the course of a call, so repeating the primary survey catches new life threats as they emerge.

options.t: Repeating it is purely a documentation formality with no clinical value
options.why: Repeating the primary survey has real clinical value, not just a paperwork purpose.

options.t: A patient's condition can change, and new life threats can emerge
The primary survey only needs to be performed a single time per call
options.why: The 'only once' framing is exactly what ongoing reassessment pushes back against.

options.t: It replaces the need for ever performing a secondary assessment
options.why: Reassessment doesn't substitute for or eliminate the need for a secondary assessment.

questions.stem: During the primary survey you find both an unmanaged airway and significant external bleeding. How should this be handled?
questions.why: Life threats found during the primary survey are managed immediately as they are found — airway, decompression, and bleeding control do not wait for the survey to finish.

options.t: Finish the full survey, then treat both
options.why: Finishing the survey first leaves identified life threats untreated meanwhile.

options.t: Complete a SAMPLE history before treating
options.why: History taking comes well after immediate life threats are addressed.

options.t: Delay treatment until vitals are obtained
options.why: Waiting on vital signs delays care the patient already visibly needs.

options.t: Treat each life threat as you identify it

questions.stem: A patient is grey and diaphoretic with mottled extremities. What does this combination most suggest?
questions.why: Grey suggests acidosis, diaphoresis suggests a cardiac component, and mottling suggests systemic hypoperfusion — together they describe a badly shocked patient.

options.t: Simple anxiety producing a benign sympathetic response
options.why: Anxiety alone does not turn a patient grey with mottled extremities.

options.t: Acidosis with a cardiac component and systemic shock
An isolated allergic reaction with no perfusion problem
options.why: An isolated allergy would not produce this grey, mottled perfusion picture.

options.t: Normal skin variation requiring no further evaluation
options.why: This combination is markedly abnormal and demands further evaluation.

questions.stem: You are 12 minutes into transport with a priority trauma patient who was stable on scene. What should be happening now?
questions.why: Reassessment means repeating the primary survey and vitals and reviewing interventions on an ongoing basis, because a patient's status can change en route.

options.t: Rechecking vitals only if something visibly changes
options.why: Deterioration is often silent. Reassessment runs on a schedule rather than waiting for something to catch your eye.

options.t: Waiting until arrival to reassess anything
options.why: Waiting for arrival misses deterioration that develops during transport.

options.t: Repeating the primary survey and vital signs
Calling the receiving facility with a full written report
options.why: The radio report matters, but it does not take the place of repeating the primary survey and vitals en route.
